posts.title: The Long Night: looking back at the year
posts.body:
Tonight is the longest night of the year in Saskatoon. The sun was up for just 7 hours 43 minutes today, so the lanterns are out along the horizon on every page of the site. It felt like the right night to look back.

Six games. Prairie Engine Works came out on October 16, and Season Ticket reached 1.0 three days later. Lombard and Scrapline joined in November, Burn Rate hit 1.0, and Funded opened its trading desk.

148 versions. Since mid-November every game publishes each new version as a release, and together the six have shipped 148 of them. Prairie Engine Works (52) and Scrapline (49) lead the way.

26 devlog posts, counting this one.

The site grew up too. In October came Play here, a page for every game and a press kit. In November the studio moved to longlight.games, with its own address for every game. Then the home page became a live sky over Saskatoon, where the sun, moon, stars and weather are the real ones, a freight train rolls past the grain elevator, and you can swipe to wind the day forward. And at the end of the month came the Longlight Passport: play a game, collect its stamp, earn badges and share your card.

Thanks for playing, and for reading. The sun's back tomorrow at 9:14 AM, and from here the days get longer.

posts.title: Prairie Engine Works gets you to the garage sooner
posts.body:
This week was about the first load. The game now opens with just what it needs, and the rest downloads quietly once the garage is up: the glossary and lessons, the trophy room, photo mode, and the races themselves for every event. The first download is down from 1,041 KB to 857 KB, and the physics hasn't changed at all.

If you're quick, a screen may show Loading… or Loading the track… for a moment, then fill in by itself. If the download fails, there's a Try again button. Trophies you win in the meantime are never lost.

Save codes are safer too. Text in a save code can only ever show as words, and a damaged save can no longer leave the game stuck on its loading screen. Your own builds come through untouched. And letting go of PUSH as an oval race ends no longer causes an error.

posts.title: Funded: day types, achievements and offline play
posts.body:
About one day in four is now a special day: a Gap open, a Fed day, a Trend day or a Trading halt. You'll see which on the card at the open. After the close, the chart marks every fill and labels what each trade made or lost. There are 11 achievements to earn, and new edges, including Insurance, Bell Clerk, Iron Stomach, Bigger Book and Deep Pockets, each with its own desk prop.

Funded now plays offline from your home screen, and the title comes up faster on a slow connection. A new Career stats card keeps count of your careers, passes, firings, best day and more. Tier 3 is rebalanced: a +$7,500 target, a $3,500 premium budget, news that follows through further, and a Theta Shield that makes options 15% cheaper.

Playing with a keyboard or a screen reader got a polish. And if your phone's date is wrong, the Daily now asks you to check it.

posts.title: Burn Rate: hints, your own motors and personal bests
posts.body:
Stuck on a job? The job sheet now has a Hint button. It names the biggest problem with the motor on your bench and the one move that helps most. It gives the direction, never a number. A hint is free after two misses on a job and always free in the Sandbox. Otherwise it costs 5% of the pay, at least 50 cr. After two misses, the report also shows a note from your partner, which you can turn off in Settings.

You can now save up to 12 motors by name on the data sheet and load them in any mode or career on your phone. Your backup code carries them too. Personal bests track your best grade and fewest firings for each job, across every career.

Three jobs also got a balance pass. And backup codes are safer: a code from a stranger can no longer run anything on your phone or freeze the game.

posts.title: Lombard: a second tab can't undo your progress
posts.body:
Until now, if you had Lombard open in two tabs, the one left in the background could later save its older copy of your shop over the progress you'd made in the other, without any warning. That's fixed.

Now, if another tab has saved since, the older tab won't save over it. Instead it covers the shop with a notice, This shop moved on in another tab, and one button: Load the newer save. The shop clock stops behind it. The check also runs when you come back to a tab, so you won't play on from an old copy.

With one tab open, nothing changes.

posts.title: Behind the build: Prairie Engine Works
posts.body:
Prairie Engine Works is the oldest game in the studio and the biggest. You design an engine part by part, put it on a dyno, find out what breaks, then take it racing. It's one web page that runs on a phone, and it has grown one small release at a time into something much larger than we planned.

It starts with the build. You pick one of nineteen layouts, from a single cylinder through inline engines, V6s, V8s (crossplane or flat-plane), V10s, V12s and flat engines to one- to four-rotor Wankels and a triangular two-stroke diesel. Then you set 73 things: bore and stroke, block and head materials, pistons, rings, rods, the crank and bearings, the valvetrain, induction and boost, the exhaust, the fuel and tune, launch control, oiling, cooling, sealing and the finish. There are 56 part tables with 268 options in all, and fifteen fuels from pump gas to methanol, propane and diesel. If you'd rather not start from nothing, there are 96 base engines. A 3D engine on a stand changes with every choice, down to belts that turn at the right speed for their pulleys.

The dyno is where you find out. There are three tests: a power pull, an endurance run to failure and an over-rev test. The sim behind them is plain code with no graphics in it, so it runs anywhere, even without a screen. It works through the air, the geometry, how well the engine breathes, the boost, fuel and ignition, then the cycle itself (four-stroke, two-stroke or rotary), the exhaust, the loads on every part, and wear. It gives you power and torque curves, a verdict, the part that failed and why, and notes from the engineer. When something breaks, the teardown panel tries every part table and a few slider steps and names the one change that fixes the failed part without breaking anything else. One tap fits it.

Then you take it somewhere. There are ten kinds of event, and each has its own sim, classes, rivals and 3D scene. The drag strip models tyres, aero, turbo heat soak, gearing and the launch. The tractor pull has a runaway sled. In the mud bog the radiator packs up. The boat drags have hulls that climb onto the plane. The salt flats have records to break, and the hill climb has 156 corners with less air at the top. There's a dirt oval and a paved one, a road course with a ghost of your best lap, and a 24-hour race with weather, fuel stops and a crew chief who can call the strategy for you. Every venue is invented: Section Line Dragway, Gumbo Flats, the Bitterwater Salt Flats, Cloudsplitter Peak.

The career is built around race teams. Each season up to five teams call, each with a driver, a series of eight rounds, a parts budget and a fee. You build their engine, certify it with a clean pull on your dyno, and they race it. A podium earns a bonus, a title earns more, and a top-two finish brings the team back next year with a bigger budget. From 300 reputation you can supply two teams at once, racing on alternate weeks. Around that sit the extras: sponsors, crew with names and moods, research projects, crate engine sales, a car show and sound-off in your off weeks, and rival shops that start feuds and, sixteen weeks later, turn up with a copy of your build. The dyno grows with you, from a 400 hp chassis dyno to a cell that measures 15,000.

The sound took nearly as long as the engines. A synthesiser builds a voice for your engine from its firing order, exhaust and intake. On top of that sit 76 openly licensed recordings of real engines and blow-offs, plus turbos that whistle and blowers that whine. At the drags, Hassan, an announcer voiced with ElevenLabs, calls the night: 143 lines, with matchup calls put together from pieces. Every venue has its own crowd and its own background sound.

A game this size needs guard rails. A regression test runs 500 numbers from ten engines, the dyno and all ten events against a stored baseline, so any change to the physics lists exactly what moved. The page is built from 127 source files, and parts that aren't needed at first load in the background so a phone gets to the garage sooner. There are three graphics tiers: Lite for phones, and Full and Ultra with baked reflections rendered in Blender. Saves fit in one backup code you can paste anywhere, and the game works offline once installed.

Prairie Engine Works is free and plays on your phone. Pick a small V8, give it a mild cam, and see how far past the redline it gets before something lets go.

posts.title: Behind the build: Frontier Lab
posts.body:
Frontier Lab is a tycoon game about running an AI company. You start with a seed round of $1.5 million, all of it yours to spend, and one city. You open a sales office, price your plans and your API, hire a team and a manager, and start signing up customers. Years later, if it goes well, you run a listed lab with offices in the world's tech capitals, data centres at energy sites, a share price, a jet and a place on the rich list. Every company, model and person in it is invented.

It didn't start as an AI game. Frontier Lab began as a fork of Vault Street, a bank tycoon we'd built, and was converted one system at a time over nine stages. Branches became sales offices, deposits and loans became recurring revenue, the treasury floor became Compute and the risk floor became Safety & Alignment. Some of the code still uses the bank names so that saves and tests kept working through the change. What made the conversion work is that an AI lab has the same shape as a bank: a lot of money moving every week, a resource you can run out of, and a regulator watching your ratio.

The money is recurring revenue. Plans, API usage, apps and enterprise contracts all add to your ARR, your annual recurring revenue, and each week the lab earns about a fifty-second of it. Every customer needs compute. Your own GPUs serve them first, then GPUs you've reserved, then the spot market, whose price follows a global chip cycle of glut, normal and shortage. Run short and new sign-ups pause. Stay short for three weeks and outages start, and customers leave.

Then there's the regulator. Your Safety ratio is the strength of your Safety & Alignment team against the risk your model carries, and a model far ahead of everyone else carries more. A strong ratio makes businesses with sensitive data prefer you. A weak one caps your dividends, then halves new sign-ups and stops you opening offices, and at the bottom stops sign-ups altogether. Stay very low for eight weeks and the regulator offers a paid pause while its monitors work with your team. Refuse and your licence is revoked for half a year. It's never game over, though. The only way to lose is to run out of cash for four weeks with no credit left.

Each sales office has five tabs. Service shows your reviews, which name real causes ("Support answered in five minutes and fixed it in ten"), and your staff and manager. Products is your price sheet: a margin ring on every plan, and a better model gives you room to charge more before customers churn. The Deal Desk is where businesses in the city send proposal requests, each with a budget, a contract length and a five-sided chart of what kind of customer they'd be. You bid a discount and see your exact chance of winning. Contracts renew at the start of each quarter, and that's when you can steal a rival's accounts. Marketing and Finance round it out.

The rivals run on the same economics as you: customers, compute, offices and a cash pile that sets their runway. They enter new cities, react to price wars, ship new models, and when their money runs out they fail, and their offices go up for sale at a discount. Once you're public you can buy them. To list, you need $100 million of ARR, four profitable quarters and a decent safety rating, among other things.

The world around the lab is simulated as well. Every country moves through booms and recessions, its central bank meets through the year, and the economy moves customer demand, business failures and share prices. The weekly newspaper, The Weekly Inference, is written from what actually happened: your openings and contract wins, rival model releases, rate decisions, elections and sports. Outside work there's a personal fortune to spend on homes, cars, a jet, art you have to check for fakes, and a sports team.

The look came from the bank game and stayed. Each city's map is printed in its own ink, like a banknote, and the buildings are engraved line drawings. The interface around them is quiet and simple. The whole simulation is deterministic: the same seed and the same decisions give exactly the same five years, and a test checks that on every change. A balance script plays ten years without a screen and compares the results with a table of targets.

Frontier Lab is off the Games page for now while it gets more work. When it comes back, start in a small city with one office and see how far one office can take you.

posts.title: Behind the build: Funded
posts.body:
Funded is a trading game that plays like a roguelike. You sit down at a desk at a trading firm with an evaluation account. Pass the firm's rules and you climb to a bigger desk. Break one, even once, and you're fired, and the next career starts from the bottom. The market is invented and the money isn't real. What we wanted to get right was the pressure.

A trading day lasts three minutes. The clock runs from the opening bell to the close, and the price ticks along a live candle chart on the monitors in front of you. You buy, you sell (shorting is allowed), or you flatten. The firm's rules sit beside the chart as meters: a profit target to reach, a daily loss limit you can't touch, and a trailing floor under your best day that rises as you do well. The floor counts your open trade as well as your banked money, so a good day can end on one bad trade. And at the closing bell you have to be flat. Hold anything past the bell and you're fired, so the last twenty seconds have a countdown.

The market is built to be fair. The whole day is worked out in advance from a seed, so a day you leave halfway through comes back at the exact same moment. Volatility is high at the open and the close and quiet in the middle. The market shifts between trending up, trending down, choppy and wild. News lands two to four times a day, and its times are marked on the clock before it arrives, so you know when it's coming but not what it says. The first jump from a headline is capped, so it can hurt you but not end your day in one tick. What happens next is up to you.

That's Tier 1. Pass it and you're promoted to a futures desk with one invented contract and whole-contract sizes. Pass that and you're trading options: one stock a day, calls and puts, with prices that decay through the day and an earnings release that pumps them up and then crushes them. Pass all three and you reach the funded account, where there's no target any more. Every five days, 80% of the week's profit is paid out as reputation and the account resets. A red week carries over. It runs until you break a rule.

The roguelike part sits between the days. After every day you survive, you pick one of three cards, called edges, and you keep it until you're fired. Some are simple, like Coffee or Stop Discipline. Some are rare, like Rewind and Tape Reader. One, Leverage Loan, is cursed: bigger sizes, a tighter loss limit. Each edge also puts a prop on your desk, so after a good run you can see your career sitting there. Once you've finished a run you can take on mandates, handicaps like No Flatten or Max Only, for more reputation. Reputation buys permanent perks that survive a firing.

Balancing that took a robot. A balance script plays thousands of evaluations with each edge and each mandate, one careful bot and one aggressive bot. It found real problems. Tape Reader took the pass rate from 8% to 57%, so it became rare and its warning got shorter. Hot Hand was a trap: a bigger max size against the same loss limit got players fired more often, so it was rebuilt. When the careful bot couldn't pass, the news was made stronger, so playing carefully is a real way to win.

The desk is rendered in Blender from a script. The room changes as you climb, from the back row to the middle of the floor to a window seat over the city. It has morning and late-afternoon light that fades across the day, a rain day now and then with streaks on the glass, and a cardboard box on the desk when you're fired. On a phone, a pointer glides to the button you tap and the mouse on the desk slides a little to match. The sounds were made with ElevenLabs.

There's a Daily Challenge too: one seeded day that's the same for everyone, with a par to beat and squares to share. The first try counts and replays are practice.

Funded is free and plays on your phone. Start with the guided first day, then try to survive five days on the back row.

posts.title: Behind the build: Lombard
posts.body:
Lombard is a pawn shop game, and it started from one question we wanted the player asking all day: what is this thing, what is it worth, and is this person lying to me? You buy a failing pawn shop cheap on a canal in Mostograd, an invented river city of drawbridges and old facades, in the 2010s. The last owner left town in a hurry, and some of the people coming through the door think the shop still owes them something.

You never leave the counter. A customer walks in, puts something on the mat, and tells you a story about it. Then it's up to you. The item lifts to eye level and you turn it in your fingers, pinch to look closer, and pick up the tools: a loupe for hallmarks and serials, a scale for weight, a magnet, a UV light that shows fresh glue and repainting, a reference book, and later an acid kit, a phone lookup and a specialist on retainer you can ring. Every tool costs time, and the line at the door doesn't wait. Push your luck and the customers at the back walk out.

The rule we held to: the game never says "FAKE". Each check gives you a finding, like "hallmark reads 583 but the stamp edges are soft", and you decide what it means. An item can be genuine, fake, restored, or what we call a frankenstein: real parts in the wrong combination. You get better at this yourself, not just your character. After a week you know which checks matter for a watch and which ones are wasted on a camera.

Then you make an offer, or a loan. Buying at about half of what a thing is worth keeps the shop alive; going much lower insults people, and overpaying for a fake is the fastest way to lose money. A pawn loan is the slow, warm money: they get cash, the item waits in the storeroom for thirty days, and if they don't come back for it, it's yours. Haggling is a few rounds, and you can bring a reason with your number: just the number, a finding as evidence, sympathy, or a threat to walk away. Each customer is stubborn, flexible, proud or desperate, and the wrong approach on the wrong person ends the deal.

There are 144 kinds of item now: gold, watches, medals, cameras, icons, phones, instruments, records, tools, sports gear, and more. Each has its own tells and its own fakes, and almost every one has a 3D model built in Blender by a script.

The people matter more than any one deal. Forty regulars come in on their own schedules and remember how you treated them. A student pawns the same laptop three times. A man swears his watches come from a friend in Dubai, until the day he brings in a real one. A grandmother needs money for her roof and has her medals with her. Eight longer stories run across a career, including a collector who wants one particular icon and will pay a fortune for it, and a canal flood that lets you be a hero or a vulture.

Lombard has a crime layer, and it's grounded. Buy something off the stolen-goods list in the morning paper and nothing happens today. Something happens in three weeks, when Detective Volkova comes in and asks about it. You can hand it over, lie, or slide her an envelope, and each one has a cost later. A polite man offers the shop "insurance"; keep saying no and one night a brick comes through the counter case. The fence on the night drawbridge buys your problems and sells you cheap goods, and he writes down every time you say no. You can run a completely clean shop. It's slower and harder, and it's a real way to play.

There's no fixed end. From day 90 you can retire, and the game reads four things it has been quietly keeping score of the whole time: how much money you made, how clean you kept it, whether you were fair to people who needed it, and who in the city respects you. That picks your title, from The Honest Lombard to Fence of Mostograd. The last newspaper writes up your career, and a card for each regular says what became of them.

The shop itself is lit by Blender, but nobody opens Blender to do it. A script builds the room, Blender works out the light in GitHub Actions, and the result is packed small enough for a phone and deployed on its own. Kelbo starts a bake from the GitHub app on his phone. Outside the window the city goes on: people walk past, a boat leaves a wake, a pigeon lands on the sill, and in winter the canal freezes.

Lombard launched on 6 November and is free to play on your phone. Start with a careful week: check everything, pay fair, and see who comes back.

posts.title: Behind the build: Season Ticket
posts.body:
Season Ticket started with one rule: you never steer a player. You own a club in the Kestrel Football League, in an invented country called Valmere, and you run all of it: tickets, sponsors, the stadium, transfers, the academy, the lineup and the tactics. On match day you set the shape and the instructions, and then you watch. You can change any of it at any moment, but the players decide for themselves what to do with the ball.

That rule only works if the players are worth watching, so most of the work went into the match engine. Every match in the league, not just yours, plays out with all 22 players and the ball moving on a full-size pitch. Your match steps ten times a second. The ones you don't watch run in a faster mode in the background, on separate threads, so the screen never freezes while the league catches up.

Tactics decide where each player wants to stand. Every slot in a formation has two spots, one for when you have the ball and one for when you don't, and some roles move between the two: a full-back who overlaps, a winger who comes inside, a midfielder who drops in between the centre-backs. The defensive line height, the press, the width, the tempo and how direct the passing is are all dials, and each one moves real players. Push the line up and press high, and you leave a gap behind the midfield that a quick striker can find.

The man on the ball weighs about forty options: a pass to each team-mate he can see, to feet or into space, a few through balls, a handful of dribbles, a shot, a cross, a clearance. Each one is worth how dangerous it makes things if it works, minus how dangerous it is if he loses the ball there. His vision, composure and positioning decide how often he picks the best one, and a tired player gets it wrong more often. A pass works if no defender can get to its path in time. Offside is judged on real positions at the moment of the pass, and fouls happen where the challenge actually happened.

One principle kept the engine honest: tune causes, never results. There is no "goals" knob. If a test season had too few goals, we changed finishing or how far the keeper could reach, never the score. Expected goals guide a player's choice to shoot and fill in the stats, but they never decide whether a shot goes in. The flight of the ball, the keeper and anyone in the way decide that. Home advantage has a cause too: a full stadium lifts the home side's play a little, and the referee leans their way on fouls.

The engine also had to give the same match on every phone. A match is saved as a recipe: the seed, the two lineups and every change made during it, by you or by the other coach. Play that recipe back and you get exactly the same match, which is how replays work without storing anyone's positions. To keep it exact, the engine sticks to plain arithmetic and does without the built-in maths functions that can differ by a hair between browsers, because on a football pitch a hair turns into a different match. A set of "golden" matches with known results runs on every change. If one of them comes out differently, the engine's version number has to go up.

Around the match sits the club. The money and the football are one system: winning sells tickets, tickets pay wages, and overspending brings the lenders. Break a loan's conditions and you start down a ladder: a warning letter, a lender's man in your finance office, a spending lock, forced sales, and at the bottom, receivership, where the bank takes the club and the career ends. The lenders only back off after four clean weeks, and they rescue a club once. Come back to them a second time and the bank takes over.

You see all of it. The office is 3D and grows with the club, from a modest room to a tower suite. The stadium is built stand by stand, with the seats in your colours. The match plays in 3D with players in a modelled kit, a town around the ground and hills on the horizon, all built in Blender from scripts. A newspaper, a fan feed, press conferences, rivalries and deadline day give each week a story.

Season Ticket launched on 19 October and has kept growing since. If you want to see the engine at its best, start a career, wait for a rainy match day, set your side to press high and watch what the wet pitch does to the first touches.

posts.title: Behind the build: Scrapline
posts.body:
Scrapline started with a promise: every loss should read as a design lesson. You build a fighting robot under a weight limit, prove it on the bench, drive it in the arena, patch it in the pit and read the post-mortem. Then you build better. If a loss only told you "you lost", the whole loop would fall apart, so most of the game exists to explain what just happened to your robot.

You start in the Haldis, a watchmaking valley in Velmark, an invented alpine country, with a plywood box in a rented corner of a machine shop. Club meets are at the valley's community hall. Later the circuit travels to the industrial towns: the steel mill at Stahlbrück, the river docks at Eisenau, the rail yards at Grauwald. At the top is the Scrapline Open, televised from the Eisenhalle. There are five weight classes, from a 150 g ant to a 110 kg heavyweight.

The weight bar is the heart of the Build tab. Every part is written once, at beetleweight scale, in grams and millimetres, the way builders think. One function turns a design into physics: mass, centre of mass, top speed, turn rate, how much energy the spinner stores, how long the battery lasts, which face is weakest. Going over the limit is impossible, so every gram is a choice: thicker front armour or a heavier disc. A stress report says what that choice costs, in plain words: this shaft will shear, that face is bare and the battery sits right behind it.

The fight is the part we're proudest of under the hood. The 3D arena doesn't decide anything. The fight is a simulation that steps sixty times a second from a seed, and the 3D view only draws what it says. Same seed, same builds, same stick inputs: same fight, every time. That's why a replay is tiny (the seed, the builds and your thumb movements), why you can scrub a replay on the cheapest phone (the game just re-runs the fight up to that moment), and why the daily challenge and replay codes work at all.

It also means the balance gets tested without a phone. A script plays every test build against every other build in its class, in that class's usual arena, across a dozen seeds, and fails if any style of robot wins much less than about a third of the time or much more than two thirds. Wedges, flippers, hammers, drums and spinners all have to stay in the fight. One build is allowed to lose: "Sloppy budget", the example of how not to build.

Hits have to land in a way you can follow. A hit on a face goes through that face's armour first. Whatever gets through hits the most exposed part behind it, so where you put the battery matters as much as what protects it. Wheels come off, motors die, discs bend, shafts shear. A wedge with a lower front edge gets underneath, and a flipper can throw a robot that lands on its back and has to right itself or be counted out. If nobody gets knocked out, the judges score it on damage, aggression and control.

Then comes the post-mortem. It opens on the result, draws your robot from above with numbered markers where it was hurt, runs a timeline of every hit with a lane for the time you spent pinned or held, and gives one redesign hint. Each problem gets two buttons: Fix it takes you to the part on the Build tab, and Test it opens the bench test that would have shown it.

The bench is the honest middle step: a drive test, a weapon test against an anvil, a swinging mass that hits each face harder until something behind it breaks, a wedge gauge, a battery run, a drop test, and since this autumn a test dummy that runs the real fight sim against three parked boxes. Your bench numbers go straight onto the build sheet, so you can see where the maths was right and where the robot surprised you.

The career grew in layers: the pit window between rounds, rivals who remember what beat them and fit a counter, sponsors whose logos go on the robot's side, a hired driver, a driving school with medals, and a highlight reel of each season's five best moments. The two voices in the arena, Duncan the announcer and Jess on commentary, were written by Kelbo and voiced with ElevenLabs: 221 lines, cued so no two ever talk over each other. The arenas, wheels, weapons and shells on the higher graphics settings were modelled in Blender from scripts, and the phone setting draws everything from code so it stays quick.

The newest work is the odd stuff: thwackbots, meltybrains, piston spears, a clamp that lifts the other robot clear of the floor, flamethrowers and a low saucer that things skate off. Each one had to fit the same sim, the same damage model and the same post-mortem as everything else.

If you want the fastest way in, open Fight, then School, and run the first drill.

posts.title: Behind the build: Burn Rate
posts.body:
Burn Rate started with one picture: a strip chart. Two lines draw across it during a test firing, the pressure you predicted, ghosted underneath, and the pressure the real motor is making. When they drift apart, you feel it before the test stand does. Everything else in the game was built to make that moment mean something.

You run a two-person rocket startup leasing a concrete stand at Site 41, a retired state test range on a salt flat. Clients bring a spec: so much total impulse, a burn time, a pressure limit, a size. You design a solid motor to meet it, choosing the grain shape, the nozzle, the case and the igniter, and the bench draws the curves you should get. Then you fire it for real, and the real motor never quite matches.

The physics underneath is real, textbook internal ballistics, the kind used to size actual motors, cut down until it runs on a phone. The burning surface of the grain, divided by the nozzle's throat, sets the chamber pressure. Pressure sets how fast the grain burns, and as the surface grows or shrinks, so does everything else. The sim steps through the burn by how much grain has burned away rather than by the clock, which keeps it stable and quick enough to redraw every curve while you drag a slider. Simple shapes like tubes and segmented grains use exact formulas. Stars, slots and the other advanced shapes are drawn on a grid and burned back one layer at a time, so any port shape works, and you can scrub through the burn to watch the surface grow.

The propellants are a deliberate choice. Every grade in Burn Rate is fictional: a name, a line of character ("forgiving, low exponent", "fast and touchy") and a block of performance numbers. There are no recipes anywhere in the game. The interesting decisions are geometric anyway: how big the port is, how much burning area you start and end with, how hard you push the case.

The gap between the bench and the stand is where the game lives. Each firing adds seeded, explainable differences to the ideal motor: this batch burns a little fast, the dawn air left the grain cold, the throat wore wider late in the burn, a small void in the grain added area all at once. Every one of them is something the range report can name. Fire at dawn and a motor runs slow and low; fire the same design at three in the afternoon and it runs fast and high. A design with a thin margin can pass in the morning and burst after lunch.

When it does burst, you get the part we care about most: the incident report. It lays the predicted and measured traces over each other, marks the moment it went wrong, and says why in one plain sentence, with the number that crossed the line. Then it gives you a button that jumps straight to the control to change. Ruslan Abenov, the range safety officer, signs it with a dry line of his own. Even a passing motor gets a "Why it differed" card that walks from the bench's prediction to what the stand measured, one cause at a time, so the rows add up exactly.

The career grows from a single small stand to booster contracts. Flight jobs put your motor on a rocket and grade it on how high it gets, with a light seeded wind on launch day. Tenders fire a lot of five motors from one design, and four have to pass. Later you lease an altitude chamber, where a big vacuum nozzle finally pays off. The hush house, Site 41's old jet-engine test building, is home base: motors are built in its bay and fired in its test cell, and the 3D range around it was modelled in Blender and baked down small enough for a phone.

Balance is tested by a bot. It plays every job from that job's starting drawing and has to deliver all 34 of them with the game's own tools. The in-game hint is the bot's own next move, given in words and never as a number, so the bench and the hint always agree.

The Daily Spec is one shared job a day with a fixed parts kit, the same for everyone. If you want to see the strip chart for yourself, it's the quickest place to start.

posts.title: Scrapline: odd weapons, rival grudges and a driving school
posts.body:
Your workshop has a lot more in it. New weapons include the eggbeater, drisk, grabber, piston spear, clamp and lift, flamethrower and a thwackbot tail. New bodies range from shell and ring spinners to a two-wheel drum and a saucer. Pick a wheel layout from casters to mecanum, add front and back attachments, and turn free tuning dials for voltage, wheel size, weight bias and tooth count.

Rivals now rebuild to counter you, a third meeting becomes a grudge match, and two new rivals join. Each regional venue has its own arena, and some arenas now have flame grates. You can name your team, pick its colours and badge, and relive big moments in slow motion or in your season's highlight reel.

A new driving school has eight drills with medals, and the new Point to go stick drives where you push.

posts.title: Prairie Engine Works: venue names, crowd sounds and a crew chief
posts.body:
Tapping Events now opens a grid of big venue cards, and the venues have names: Section Line Dragway, Gumbo Flats, Sundog Speedway and more. The salt flats are now Bitterwater Salt Flats and the big hill is Cloudsplitter Peak, and your records carry over. Each venue has its own background sound, and the crowd cheers, claps, gasps or groans at the finish.

In the 24 Hours, a crew chief can now call the pit strategy for you. Every event's auto driver got quicker. Watch it replays now cover pull, bog, boat and hill teams. The throttle slider works like a pedal that starts the engine.

New players get a four-step career tour, and class limits now show before you sign or pay to certify. On Full and Ultra, engines gain modelled parts and real cast and machined finishes. The first run of an event no longer freezes.

posts.title: New game: Funded, trade your way up without getting fired
posts.body:
Funded is our newest game, now on longlight.games. You sit at a trading desk on a five-day evaluation. Hit the profit target without breaking the daily loss limit or the trailing drawdown, and hold nothing at the closing bell, or you're fired. A guided training day walks you through it first.

Pass and you're promoted, from stocks to a futures desk to a $100k options desk, each with a better seat on the floor. After each day you survive, pick one of three edge cards for the rest of your career. You can spend Reputation on perks like Newswire or a Mulligan. Optional mandates make a career harder for more Reputation.

The trading floor has its own sounds and music, and about one day in five it rains.

posts.title: Lombard: more time to think, and three new things to appraise
posts.body:
Three new items have come through the door: army field binoculars, a brass ship's barometer and a programmable calculator. That makes 144 things to appraise.

We watched new players at the counter and made the shop kinder to them. While you inspect or price an item, the clock stops on your first day and runs at half speed after that. Customers in line wait a little longer, and tapping the waiting count shows how patient each one is. Tools now show their cost in shop minutes.

Pricing is easier to learn too. Once you look an item up in the reference book, the estimate pad shows the book's range, and your first item's range is free. The day's ledger says whether each buy was real or fake and roughly what it was worth. Selling to the dealer now shows the price and asks before it sells.

posts.title: Prairie Engine Works: more to tune, weather and a rival feud
posts.body:
The drag setup has a lot more to play with: two-step rpm and launch retard, custom gear ratios, a shift rpm slider, ride height and converter stall. Three saved tunes let you swap setups between passes, and the timing slip shows how each split changed from your last clean pass. The truck pull and the road course get their own new sliders, and the road and pull sheets now suggest a setup change. Hill and pull teams race with your setup.

Road, hill and pull days now have weather, rain included. A rival shop can start a feud with you, trash-talking and copying your build until you beat it in head-to-heads. You can also sell crate engines for side income.

There's a throttle slider next to Start, an announcer calls the drag strip, and real 3D props fill the garage, pull track and pits on Full and Ultra.

posts.title: Scrapline: body styles, weapon bays and a voiced arena
posts.body:
Your robot's chassis now comes in seven body styles, from a plain box to a dome, pancake or invertible. Weapons sit in real bays cut into the body. An open bay is also a weak spot, so a hammer from above can hit your weapon first.

The fight screen is easier to read. The camera follows the action, and each bot gets a card showing its parts, bars and worst damage. An announcer and a commentator call the fights, and there's a crowd, bells and a set of new hit sounds.

There's a home screen with Career and Sandbox modes, plus a daily challenge that's the same for everyone and replay codes you can share. Opponents drive smarter, and flippers now throw bots further in the small classes.

posts.title: Lombard: voices, new sounds and more to buy
posts.body:
Customers at Lombard's counter now talk. About half say hello when they walk in, and they react out loud to your offers. A handful of story characters have their own voices.

The shop sounds more alive: the shutter going up and down, the morning paper, a ringing phone, rain on the street, a tram bell and a wax-sealed stamp when you write a pawn.

There are 141 things to appraise now, with a new sports category: skates, a signed puck, boxing gloves and a chess clock. Each has its own 3D model. Pawn tickets, a landscape layout and keyboard shortcuts for desktop are in too.

posts.title: Two new games, new addresses and a studio sting
posts.body:
Two games joined the lineup this week. Lombard is a pawn shop sim on a canal in Mostograd: spot the fakes, haggle and decide how much trouble a good deal is worth. Scrapline has you design, drive and patch a combat robot.

The studio now lives at longlight.games, and every game has its own address, like pew.longlight.games for Prairie Engine Works. Games also ask the browser to keep their saves when a phone runs low on space.

Covers and screenshots are twice as sharp on big phones, and version numbers now have four parts, so every small build shows. There's a Sound switch at the bottom of every page too. It's off by default; turn it on and the Longlight sting plays once per visit as the logo's sun rises. The sun moves more now as well: its glow breathes, a low sun wobbles near sunset, and tapping it sends a lens flare across the sky.

posts.title: Prairie Engine Works: more team offers and a steadier garage camera
posts.body:
The Team tab now shows five offers at once, and no two are the same kind of racing. Some teams are shoestring outfits and some are well funded. About half carry a rule, like pump fuel only, iron block, no power adders or an engine size cap. Rules pay a little more, and they go on your race-day checklist.

Anyone who picked Synth or Blend as their engine voice keeps that choice. We also fixed the garage camera: zoomed all the way out, it no longer pokes through the walls or props. The panel now stays at whatever height you drag it to.

On Full and Ultra, cars now have open windows, a cabin and a driver. Belts and pulleys no longer look like they're running backwards at high revs. Ultra also now gets the shadowing and glow it was always meant to have.

posts.title: Prairie Engine Works: race teams and real engine sounds
posts.body:
The career now runs race teams instead of selling engines. Take on team offers, build three engines a season and run series in mud bog, boat drag, truck and tractor pull and hill climb, with Pikes Peak as the finale. Drivers remember you, rival shops build cars for your series, and from 300 rep you can run two teams at once. Watch it replays your team's race in 3D, and the off weeks bring a car show and a sound-off.

Real recordings are now the default engine voice. Rotaries, V4s, singles, twins and inline 5s got their own recordings, plus a new V12 rev and recorded blow-off, backfire and anti-lag bangs.

The garage also got a glass look: floating tab bar, glass panels and popups, swipe between tabs, a live dyno curve on the workshop monitor and a full-screen results card you can share.

posts.title: Frontier Lab: the whole lab is playable
posts.body:
Frontier Lab has grown from a map and a title screen into a full AI-lab tycoon. Raise a seed round, open a sales office in each city, buy compute or build data centers, train and launch your own models (open weights too), win public-sector tenders, and keep an eye on rival labs and the safety regulator.

The last week was audit and polish: pacing, popups and navigation, more incidents, news and tips for the late game, a rescaled rich list and a yearly annual report. It's at version 0.1.61 and still in development.

posts.title: Play here, game pages and a press kit
posts.body:
Three new things on the site this week.

Every game page now has a Play here button. It opens the game right inside the page, over the whole screen, with a Close button on top. The phone's Back button closes it too.

Each game also has its own address now, like game-prairie-engine-works.html. Share one of those in a text or on Discord and the preview shows that game's cover and summary.

And there's a press kit, with our logo, colours, and every game's cover and screenshots, for anyone writing, filming or streaming about our games. It's linked at the bottom of every page.

posts.title: Season Ticket hits 1.0
posts.body:
Season Ticket, our soccer club management game, is out as version 1.0. Own a club in the 16-team Kestrel Football League, run the business from your own 3D office, build the squad and the stadium, and change tactics while you watch the match.

It plays a whole career on your phone, even offline.

posts.title: Prairie Engine Works is out
posts.body: Our biggest game so far is released. Put an engine together on the test stand, fire it up and hear it run, then take it to the drag strip or a truck and tractor pull to earn cash and reputation.
